catalog_quote: Basically, the primary stress in any word falls on the first syllable, with secondary stress on the third syllable of a four-syllable root or a trisyllabic word carrying a monosyllabic suffix and/or on the first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme, or on the first of a pair of bound monosyllabic morphemes if it does not tend to form a diphthong or long vowel with the preceding vowel (i.e. is not -yi after /a/ or /i/). A non-productive stem formative (like -lu in parrkulu 'two') is not treated as a bound morpheme but as part of the root. Secondary stresses are not always detectable. ... An alternative for words like the last example above, with a monosyllabic suffix preceding a disyllabic, is to have the secondary stress on the monosyllabic suffix ... the only other vowel-initial bound morpheme, the emphatic marker -ardi, is stressed on its first syllable and often even carries the…

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed initial primary stress, weight-blind; morphologically conditioned secondary stress; listed lexical/morphological exceptions such as -ardi and distorted final vowels; phrase stress separate) rests on the standard and only reference grammar of the language, Breen 2004 (PL 558), sec. 3.6, and every deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim on the page scan we hold (p.30) and held scanned text (p.31, p.33). Glottolog lists nothing better (the other items are a duplicate record, an unpublished Breen ms absorbed into the grammar, an unpublished Nhirrpi dialect sketch, and 19th-c./missionary sketches); Crossref and lingbuzz show no phonology/prosody study; the language is extinct so no instrumental work is expected. Only nit: the locator should read printed pp.30-33 (3.6.1 Phrase stress starts on p.33), not pp.30-32. no reclassification, no upgrade needed (grade is already page-image)

sources.note: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable: confirms the catalog initial stress. Secondary stress is morphological, not purely rhythmic: 3rd syllable of a 4-syllable root or of trisyllabic word + monosyllabic suffix, first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme, first of a pair of bound monosyllabic morphemes (unless it coalesces with the preceding vowel, e.g. -yi after /a/ or /i/); examples tjukurru-li or tjukurru-li 'kangaroo-ERG' (either) and 'fat-CHAR-INCH-CONT' with a variant placing the secondary on the monosyllabic suffix. sources.quote: Breen (1975:7) provides some details regarding the distribution of the voiced stops. He says of the voicing contrast: 'The distinction is found only after stressed vowels (and almost always after a primary stressed vowel) or in nasal-stop clusters.' || In summary, the Yandrruwandha system seems to be: (a) an intervocalic contrast for stops after the first (stressed) vowel of a word, except for apico-alveolar
sources.note: Incidental and second-hand (quoting Breen 1975 manuscript). Austin equates the primary-stressed vowel with the first vowel of the word, consistent with the catalog's fixed initial rule. Breen's wording 'stressed vowels (and almost always after a primary stressed vowel)' implies non-primary stressed vowels exist, i.e. some secondary stress, which the catalog rule string (no secondary marks) does not show; too indirect to bind as a refinement.

tone.summary: Whole sketch grammar searched (phonology sec. 2 read in full): no mention of tone, pitch or intonation. Phonology covers consonants, clusters, prestopping, three vowels, vowel length and stress (initial primary, secondary on third syllable); almost identical to Innamincka Yandruwantha (Breen 1975).
